cells.tense: You're at the table with the pen, and the thing you just pulled down you pulled down on purpose.
cells.ask: Pick one small practice and keep it for a week — same twenty minutes, same place — not because it's working yet, but to let the repetition do the refining while you stand on the cleared ground.
cells.core:
Something false gave way and you're standing in the space it left. You chose the collapse, or at least you didn't flinch from it, and the clearing held. Nothing dramatic in the aftermath — you just know which way you're facing, and it isn't a guess.

What's free to grow next is the smaller thing: not another break but the plain upkeep of a practice, same twenty minutes, same chair, same quiet, so the refining happens under your feet instead of in front of your eyes. That's what a kept direction feeds on — not more revelation, just a steady light you're willing to tend. Sticking with something small buys back more room than the next clean sweep would.
cells.sheetLine: You cleared what couldn't hold and kept your footing. Now the small upkeep carries it.
cells.verb: clearing away what can't hold — a false structure falls all at once
cells.place: in the part of a life where direction gets chosen and kept to

cells.tense: You're braced for the next collapse before it's due, and the week ahead is already crowded with things that haven't happened.
cells.ask: Pick one structure you were about to tear down — a routine, a promise, a plan — and leave it standing this week, flaws and all, so time can show you what actually can't hold.
cells.core:
You're taking things down ahead of schedule. Something cracks and you finish the job before the crack has shown you what it's for — a routine ends, a promise gets pre-apologised, a plan is dropped the day it gets slightly inconvenient. The tearing-down feels like clarity from where you sit. From outside, it looks like nothing is allowed to stand long enough to be tested.

Direction needs a floor to push off. Pick one thing you were about to pull down, leave it alone for a week, and let it stand, flawed as it is. Something old and shared — a family habit, a working method, a group's way of doing things — can hold you while you find out whether the thing is broken or only uncomfortable. This week the waiting is the work.
cells.sheetLine: You're pulling things down before they've proved whether they need to go.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that closed a while back, steadying something that already fell.
cells.ask: Put up one small structure this week — a regular time, a list on a single page, one rule you actually keep — not to fix the future, but to give your direction something solid to land on.
cells.core:
There's a structure behind you that already stopped holding. You're holding it anyway — a job, a relationship, a version of yourself — and the upkeep takes the attention that would otherwise go into choosing a direction. You can see that it's over. You keep walking back to the doorway all the same, checking whether it's really finished.

What direction needs from you isn't more effort pressed into the tired place. It's a container. Put one small structure in place and keep it — a regular time, a single page of plans, one rule you follow — and let that be where your energy stands for now. Something as unremarkable as a standing Tuesday can hold a decision that would otherwise keep slipping. It's quieter than a break, and it's the one that lets the next one arrive.
cells.sheetLine: You're propping up something that already fell, and the effort keeps direction out of reach.

cells.tense: You're in a room that's already mid-change, pen down, watching it happen to you.
cells.ask: Say out loud to one person that something you've been calling stable is actually finished, and let that spoken fact choose your next move.
cells.core:
You've been talking about what's happening as if it arrived on its own. A thing is coming apart around you — trust, a commitment, an assumption you've been running on — and you describe it as something that landed, not as something you're part of. That's what most people do right up until the day it's obvious. But you're already in it, already shaping how it lands by what you notice and what you don't.

Start with one sentence. Not to fix anything — just to name what you're actually oriented toward, so your direction comes from what you genuinely see instead of from the momentum of not looking. A plain line to someone who'll take it is the move. The named thing is smaller than the version you've been braced for; that's usually how it turns out. What follows is a step that's yours.
cells.sheetLine: You're already inside the change. Saying so out loud makes it a choice you made.

attempts.check: The record does not say whether the person is actually deciding well now, only what the capacity looks like when it is operating; the reader could reasonably say a good stretch of choosing does not prove the rest of life is settled. The asks are experiments in the world — let a collapse land, name the ground, put up one shelf at a time, admit one old rule is finished — so they still teach the person something if my read is wrong about which part of their life is frozen. The sentence that serves the writer most is the closing line of the Too Much core; it wants a little pressure so the person quitting becomes a relief rather than an indictment, and that pressure is the one I watched hardest.

attempts.check: The record does not establish that any particular structure in this person's life is actually false — only what Breakthrough looks like when it is operating cleanly in the choosing capacity. A reader might fairly say they have torn nothing down recently, and the reading would be describing someone else; the asks survive that, because each is a small experiment — keep a practice a week, leave one thing standing, put up one regular time, say one finished sentence aloud — that teaches something either way. The sentence that most serves the writer rather than the reader is the Too Much closing about waiting being the work; it wants to sound earned rather than assigned, and I cut it back rather than let it swell.
